angle: D1 evidence-index — the page is an index of evidence: each project enters by its single strongest verifiable claim plus the artifact or number that proves it, and the page's structure (order, depth, what is even said) follows what can be proven rather than what looks balanced.
thesis: This design bets that making evidence a required, typed field of every project assertion — so an unbacked claim does not compile and the reader can audit the whole ledger on a public page — buys more credibility with a screening engineer than any amount of polish, and it accepts the cost that the resulting order puts the operator's most impressive-sounding result last.

routes.purpose: The index. Header, one paragraph of what the operator builds, then the five projects ordered by how independently a reader can check them — each row is name + the literal status string from its README + one claim + one evidence affordance + a link into its dossier. No images here: the index is text and numbers, which keeps the entry view the lightest one on the site.

routes.purpose: The router's mandatory `fallback` prop. Renders a 404 page with a link home. Counted in routeCount even though it occupies no path, so the E8 count is conservative rather than favourable to me.

evidenceModel: Every assertion about a project is a typed `Claim` in `src/content.ts` whose `evidence` field is REQUIRED — under TS strict an unbacked claim does not compile, so M1 is enforced by the toolchain rather than by discipline. `Evidence` is a discriminated union of five kinds, ordered by how independently a reader can check it: `live` (open the running thing yourself — climx), `number` (a value + the named instrument that produced it + the repo doc that records it — PHarvard's vendor-toolchain figures), `figure` (an artifact the project itself produced, rendered on the page and linked at full size — the PhyriadFG TikZ diagrams, the Phyriager annotated frame), `doc` (a specific file in the project's repo), and `provisional` (the project's own published statement that its numbers must NOT be cited as validated — Phynned). Project name and status are modelled as claims too, so M1's enumeration unit is covered end to end: the name's evidence is the repo URL, the status's evidence is the README the literal string was copied from. Nothing about a project renders as free prose — `<EvidenceChip>` is the only component that prints a claim's backing, which makes "rendered assertion" and "evidence affordance" the same JSX node by construction. The mechanism is instrumented twice: `src/content.test.ts` walks every project, asserts each claim carries evidence, asserts every URL is https, and asserts every `figure.file` actually exists on disk under `public/` (Node fs inside Vitest), so a broken image cannot ship; `src/pages/ProjectPage.test.tsx` renders all five dossiers and asserts that each claim's text is accompanied in the DOM by an anchor or a number. `/evidencia` then renders that same array as a public ledger, so the reader audits exactly what the tests enforce. Where a project has no checkable evidence, the design's answer is to delete the claim, not to keep it and dim the wording.

metricSelfEstimates.estimate: 100%, by construction rather than by care — but CONDITIONAL on contentGap 1. `Claim.evidence` is a required field of a discriminated union, so an assertion with no backing fails `tsc --noEmit`; `EvidenceChip` is the only component that prints backing, so every rendered assertion and its affordance are the same node. Name and status are modelled as claims (evidence = repo URL and README URL respectively), which covers M1's full enumeration unit. The conditional: if a project's GitHub repo is not public, its `repo`/`doc` evidence does not resolve, the quality veto fires, and the honest response is to delete those claims — which lowers what the page says, not the fraction. The operator's profile paragraph and the skills table are assertions about the person, not about a project, so they sit outside M1's unit; I flag that rather than let it pass as coverage.
metricSelfEstimates.instrument: `npm test` — src/content.test.ts enumerates every claim and asserts evidence present, https URLs, and that every figure.file exists on disk under public/ (Node fs in Vitest); src/pages/ProjectPage.test.tsx renders all five dossiers and asserts each claim's text is accompanied by an anchor or a number in the DOM. Plus a manual DOM read of / and one /proyecto/:slug in `npm run preview`.

contentGaps: Repository publicity is unverifiable from disk and is the single biggest threat to this design. Phynned's own README says its release link will be 'published once the project's public repository is up; until then, build from source' — i.e. github.com/Swately/Phynned may not exist publicly, while src/content.ts already links it. Phyriager's and PhyriadFG's public status is likewise unconfirmed (PHarvard's README states its URL explicitly and climx is demonstrably live). Any non-public repo means that project's claims are not one click from evidence for an external reader: the quality veto fires and M1 cannot reach 100% while those claims remain. Needs the operator to confirm or publish; the design's fallback is deleting the unverifiable claims, which makes the page shorter and thinner.

The portfolio itself has no public source. E6 records a local git repo with no remote and no commits, and no deployment URL is chosen (vite base assumes /portfolio/). The /evidencia section 'Cómo está hecha esta página' makes claims about this page — 2 runtime dependencies, hand-rolled router ported from climx — with nowhere to link them. Until the repo is pushed, that section is the one place on the site that asserts without proof, which is precisely what the design forbids elsewhere.

climx contradicts itself on the test count: its README says '41 tests' while MEASUREMENTS.md's latest dated row (2026-07-31) says 51/51. Printing either number contradicts one of that project's own sources and trips the quality veto. Needs the operator to reconcile climx's README before any test count is rendered; my design avoids the number for now, which costs the climx card its most concrete engineering figure.

climx's live Lighthouse figures (Performance 90 / Accessibility 100 home; 100 / 98 municipio) were measured against https://swately.github.io/project-tw/ BEFORE the repo rename. They are the strongest presentation numbers in the whole pool and this design refuses to print them un-rerun. A re-run against the current URL does not exist on disk.

No photograph of the PHarvard board or its display. PHarvard's strongest line — the four-digit display is produced by four calls to its own software divide routine, so 'the display is a photograph of its own software arithmetic working' — is exactly the claim a photo would prove in one glance, and there is no image of it anywhere in the project (the only PNGs under PHarvard are Lattice toolchain temp files). This is minutes of work for the operator and it is the highest-value missing asset for this design specifically.

No screenshot of climx running, of Phynned's UI, or of PhyriadFG presenting frames. climx compensates with a live URL, which is stronger than a screenshot. Phynned ends up with NO visual evidence and no citable number at all — its dossier is a claim about measurement discipline plus a link to a document that disclaims itself. That is the honest position, and it is thin.

Per-claim deep links into each repo (e.g. sw/hwcheck.s, docs/reports/EMPIRICAL_EVIDENCE_SUMMARY.md, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) are what makes the `doc` evidence kind worth anything. Those paths exist on disk and I verified several; their GitHub URLs depend on gap 1 and on each repo's default branch name, which I did not verify for any project.

Language: O2 fixes the page in Spanish, but every status string it quotes, every README it links, and every document title in the ledger is in English. The evidence rows will read bilingual by construction and there is no Spanish source to point at. This is a consequence of a recorded operator decision, not a defect, but it is a real content gap for a design whose entire surface is quotations of sources.

weakestPoint: Ordering by provability is not ordering by relevance, and this design knowingly optimizes the wrong one for its own named workload. The index leads with climx (a municipal weather site) and PHarvard (a 2.08 MHz FPGA CPU) because their evidence is the strongest a reader can check — one runs in your browser, the other reports vendor-toolchain numbers and a self-computed on-silicon verdict. The two projects that actually match the profile line the reader just read, 'infraestructura de alto rendimiento y de agentes LLM', sit third and fourth, because their evidence is a diagram and a screenshot. And Phynned — whose +98% average-FPS result is the single most impressive-sounding number the operator owns — is rendered last, with a chip that says the dataset is provisional and must not be cited, because that is what its own README says. The objective's named workload gives a screening engineer roughly twenty seconds; in twenty seconds this page can plausibly read as 'weather website and a toy processor'. I take that trade because P1 (credibility) outranks everything below it and because a reader who has seen ten inflated portfolios rewards the one that grades its own evidence — but the trade is real, it costs exactly the thing the ~20 s design target cares about, and the objective does not reward me for it anywhere, since honesty-of-ordering is not a metric while M2 (which I would score 5/5 under any ordering) is. A secondary weakness, stated so an adversary does not have to find it: /evidencia is the least load-bearing of the three routes — a reader may never open it — so it is the first thing I would cut under scope pressure, and cutting it would take the design from 16 files to about 14 without touching M1, M2 or M6.
